intro.html: History is full of people who broke from the group: lone thinkers, deserters, protesters, rebels at sea and in the hills. These words name them, and the uprisings and splits they caused.

People: dissident (speaks out), insurgent (fights), renegade (deserts), maverick (goes their own way), iconoclast (attacks cherished beliefs). Uprisings: mutiny (by sailors or soldiers), insurrection (a violent uprising), sedition (words that stir one up). Splits and sides: faction, partisan.
Notice the tone. A maverick or an iconoclast can be admired; a renegade or an insurgent usually is not. The same person may be a dissident to the government and a hero to the crowd.

words.def: a person who openly disagrees with an official policy or ruling group
words.ex: The old kingdom jailed any {dissident} who spoke out against the king’s harsh taxes.
words.ctx: Most members of the club went along with the new rules, but one {dissident} stood up at every meeting to argue that they were unfair.
words.etym: From Latin dissidere, “to sit apart, to disagree”: dis- (apart) + sedere (to sit).

mn.cue: DIS-SID: SITS APART from the crowd
mn.text: When the whole hall stands to cheer the king’s new tax, Lin stays in her seat with her arms crossed; she sits apart, a {dissident}.

scene.alt: In a hall where everyone stands and cheers, one woman stays seated holding a sign that says no.

words.def: a rebel who fights against a government or those in power
words.ex: In the old tale, the {insurgents} hid in the mountains and raided the baron’s supply wagons.
words.ctx: The rebel band was small, but the {insurgents} knew every path through the hills, and the king’s soldiers could never catch them.
words.etym: From Latin insurgere, “to rise up”: in- (against) + surgere (to rise).

mn.cue: IN-SURGE: SURGE UP against the rulers
mn.text: In the old story, the hill folk surge up the slope toward the cruel baron’s castle, waving their banner; each of them is an {insurgent}.

labels.text: IN-SURGE: RISE UP against the RULER

scene.alt: A determined band of villagers with a banner marches toward a castle.

words.def: a rebellion, especially by sailors or soldiers against their officers
words.ex: Tired of moldy biscuits, the sailors staged a {mutiny} and locked the captain in his cabin.
words.ctx: The crew had sailed for months without pay, so when the captain ordered them around the stormy cape, they refused and seized the ship in a {mutiny}.

mn.cue: MUTE-iny: the crew won’t stay MUTE
mn.text: On the fishing boat, the ship’s cats, fed up with sardines, take over the wheel and steer for the cheese island while the captain splutters; it is a {mutiny}!

scene.alt: Two cats take over a ship’s wheel while the shocked captain shouts for order.

words.def: a violent uprising against a government or authority
words.ex: The governor sent troops to put down the {insurrection} in the northern provinces.
words.ctx: What began as a peaceful march over the price of bread grew into an armed {insurrection}, and for a month the rebels held the capital.
words.etym: From Late Latin insurrectio, from insurgere (to rise up).

mn.text: In Pip’s dream, the little chess pawns rise up all at once and chase the king right off the board; it is an {insurrection}.

labels.text: IN-SURRECT: RISE UP against the KING

scene.alt: A row of small chess pawns charges at a big chess king wearing a crown, while a boy watches in surprise.

words.def: speech or action that stirs people to rebel against a government
words.ex: The printer was arrested for {sedition} after publishing pamphlets urging people to overthrow the king.
words.ctx: In the old kingdom, even a joke about the queen could be punished as {sedition}, so people learned to whisper their complaints.
words.etym: From Latin seditio, “a going apart, a revolt”: sed- (apart) + itio (a going).

mn.cue: SAID-ition: words SAID to stir a revolt
mn.text: Standing on a crate in the market, Rex shouts for the crowd to rise up against the queen; words like that are {sedition}.

scene.alt: A man on a crate shouts through a megaphone for the crowd to rise up against the queen.

words.def: a person who deserts a group or cause, or who breaks the rules
words.ex: The {renegade} knight left the king’s army and joined the outlaws in the forest.
words.ctx: Once the team’s star, he became a {renegade} in the fans’ eyes when he quit in the middle of the season to play for their fiercest rival.
words.etym: From Spanish renegado, from Medieval Latin renegatus (one who has denied): re- + negare (to deny).

mn.text: In the night, Sir Dev slips out through the castle gate and runs to join the outlaws in the woods; he is a {renegade}.

labels.text: RAN from the GATE: a DESERTER

scene.alt: At night, a young knight sneaks out of the castle gate and runs toward the forest.

words.def: an independent person who does not go along with the group
words.ex: A {maverick} among bakers, Nell puts pickles in her chocolate cake.
words.ctx: While every other architect was designing glass towers, Ada was a {maverick}, building homes of mud brick and straw that stayed cool without air conditioning.
words.etym: From the name of a Texas rancher of the 1800s who did not brand his calves; an unbranded calf came to be called a maverick.

mn.cue: the CALF that goes its OWN WAY
mn.text: Every cow in the herd plods toward the barn, but one young calf trots off the other way to explore the hill; it is a {maverick}.

scene.alt: Three cows walk toward the barn while one small calf happily heads the other way.

words.def: a person who attacks cherished beliefs or traditions
words.ex: The young chef was an {iconoclast} who served dessert first and breakfast for dinner.
words.ctx: In a field that treated tradition as sacred, the scientist was an {iconoclast}, publicly questioning ideas her own teachers had called beyond doubt.
words.etym: From Greek eikon (image) + klastes (breaker): it first named people who broke religious images.

mn.text: While the whole town bows to the old statue, Lila holds up a sign asking why, and says the town’s favorite traditions are silly; she is an {iconoclast}.

scene.alt: A teen holds up a sign asking why beside a town statue that an old man bows to.

words.def: a small group within a larger one, often at odds with the rest
words.ex: The chess club split into two {factions}: those who wanted a tournament and those who wanted pizza nights.
words.ctx: Within the town council, a small {faction} refused to approve the budget, and its stubbornness delayed the new bridge by a whole year.
words.etym: From Latin factio, “a group acting together,” from facere (to do).

mn.cue: FACTION: a group that splits OFF
mn.text: At the bake-sale meeting, two kids march to their own corner, insisting on cookies while everyone else wants cupcakes; they are a {faction}.

labels.text: FACTION: a group WITHIN a group

scene.alt: Three children cheer for cupcakes while two others stand apart with arms crossed, insisting on cookies.

words.def: strongly supporting one side, often without fairness
words.ex: The {partisan} crowd booed every call that went against the home team.
words.ctx: A fair referee must never be {partisan}; if she favors one team, the whole game becomes meaningless.
words.etym: From French partisan, from Italian partigiano, from parte (part, side).
words.note: Bipartisan means involving both major political parties. As a noun, a partisan is a strong supporter of one side, or a fighter in a resistance group.

mn.text: Grandpa wears his team’s colors from hat to socks, cheers every play for his side and boos every call against it; he is {partisan}.

scene.alt: A grandfather in his team’s red colors boos the referee, who shrugs.

after.html: Partisan means strongly for one side; bipartisan means involving both major parties, and nonpartisan means taking no side at all.

items.q: Which word is most likely to be used as praise?
items.why: A maverick is an independent thinker, often admired. Renegade and insurgent usually blame; sedition is a crime.

items.q: The sailors refused their captain’s orders and took over the ship. This was a…
items.why: A rebellion by sailors or soldiers against their officers is a mutiny.

items.q: A judge who favors one side is…
items.why: Partisan means strongly for one side. Impartial and nonpartisan mean taking no side.
eikon (image) + klastes (breaker): an iconoclast breaks cherished images and beliefs.
